Gin offerings began, by most accounts, with George Lycurgus of the Volcano House hotel, and some Hawaiians consider alcohol inappropriate, so nod to the ʻōhelo, not the gin. Read as fire and red berry: tart cranberry/pomegranate/hibiscus, ginger or chili heat, a smoky edge; striking red. Treat the lore with care. Respect: this is a deity in living Hawaiian religion and culture. Read the domain the god governs, never caricature the god, and keep the god's name out of the drink name and out of jokes ('angry god', 'sacrifice', 'virgin').
taglineWords: with the first berry set aside

concepts.reading: Hula: Hawaiian dance and storytelling (Laka is its goddess; hula kahiko is the ancient form, ʻauana the modern). The 'hula girl' dashboard image is a mid-century stereotype: read hula as grace, rhythm and story, not sexualized kitsch. Deliver a graceful, balanced, mid-strength drink: floral, gently sweet, swaying between lime and passion fruit; plumeria/orchid garnish.

A generic 'tiki god' request means the mid-century bar fantasy (carved figures from Marquesan, Māori and Hawaiian kiʻi traditions used as décor). Read it as golden-age theatrical tiki, a carved mug and a serious multi-rum drink, while keeping sacred names and 'curse/sacrifice' jokes out of names.

Māui: pan-Polynesian trickster hero who fished up islands and, from Haleakalā, lassoed the sun to slow it so the day would be longer. (Also the island name; a bare 'Maui' usually means the island: lean on upcountry Maui, pineapple fields, sunrise at Haleakalā.) Read as a long, sunny day: a golden, slow-sipping punch, pineapple and passion fruit, sunrise colors. Don't name the drink after the hero.
taglineWords: for a day that won't end

concepts.reading: Surf culture, born in Hawaiʻi (heʻe nalu), spread by Duke Kahanamoku. Read as refreshing, salty, bright and sessionable: a long, lime-forward highball or swizzle with ginger or coconut water and a saline edge; nothing heavy or creamy.
Surfers' dawn patrol: up before sunrise for glassy waves. Read as a bright, low-proof morning drink: coffee-cold-brew highball or a sunrise citrus spritz; light, awake, no cream.

Duke Kahanamoku (1890–1968): Olympic swimming champion (1912 gold) and the ambassador of surfing. Read as a classic Waikīkī beach-boy drink: clean, athletic, elegant; a light rum and pineapple-lime sour with a sparkling lift.

The ʻukulele, adapted from the Portuguese machete brought by Madeiran immigrants (1879); popularly 'jumping flea', though Queen Liliʻuokalani glossed it as 'the gift that came here'. Read as small, bright, cheerful and simple: a four-ingredient sour, light rum, lime, a fruity syrup, served up and short.

The lei: a garland given in welcome, love or farewell, of plumeria, pīkake (jasmine), tuberose, orchid, or the vanilla-scented maile vine. Read as floral and fragrant, a welcome drink: light rum or gin, lime, honey or elderflower, orange-flower water; orchid garnish.

The Samoan fire-knife dance (siva afi), the climax of Polynesian revues. Read as dramatic and fiery: a flaming garnish (spent lime shell with overproof, lit and extinguished before drinking), ginger and chili warmth, red-gold.

Volcano: fire, heat, red, smoke. Two honest readings: (1) the Volcano Bowl, a communal punch with overproof burning in the central crater; (2) a fiery drink: chili or ginger heat, smoky rum or mezcal, red fruit. Colors red-black. (Lava Flow is also a strawberry-banana colada classic.)

A request for actual fire. Tiki's flames: overproof in a spent lime shell, a lemon-extract-soaked crouton, a flamed Volcano Bowl crater, cinnamon sparked over the flame. Choose a drink whose structure supports it (zombie, bowl, hot coffee grog) and say to extinguish before drinking. Overproof is for the shell, not more booze in the glass.
Torch- or firelit evenings: smoke and warmth. Read as a smoky-sweet evening drink: Demerara or a touch of mezcal, honey, spice; amber glow; a flame only if asked.

Mermaids: shimmering, sea-green-blue, pearl and sea-foam. Read as delicate, saline-kissed and pale aqua: light rum or gin, lime, coconut water, a little lychee or elderflower, a saline drop, a foam 'sea-spray' cap. If blue is used (blue curaçao), keep every other ingredient clear so it stays aqua.

Sirens: luring song, danger under beauty. Read as seductive and dangerous: floral-fruity on top, a strong dark-rum undertow, a bitter last note. (Shannon Mustipher's Song of the Siren is a catalogue drink; don't reuse that name.)

Sharks in tiki: Vic's Shark's Tooth, Don's Tiger Shark. Read as bracing and bitey: overproof Jamaican or Demerara heat, plenty of lime, a red grenadine 'blood' plume; short and sharp. Never name it Shark's Tooth, Shark Bite or Tiger Shark (existing drinks).

Wrecks: storm, salt, timber, survival with the rum casks. Read as dark, briny, rum-heavy and storm-tossed: navy or Demerara rum, lime, honey, a saline edge, maybe ginger; barrel mug. (Trader Sam's 'Shipwreck on the Rocks' is bourbon-agave-lemon-mint.)

Pirate treasure: gold, chests, maps. Read as golden and rich: aged rum, passion fruit or honey gold, a little spice, a gold-coin orange wheel. Color is genuinely gold (passion fruit, pineapple, honey, aged rum), never blue or green.

Golden-age piracy (1650–1730): rum, gunpowder, Caribbean ports. Read as a hearty rum grog: navy/Jamaican rum, lime, dark sugar, spice; a barrel or skull mug; strong. Avoid bottle-of-rum clichés in the tagline beyond one wink.

Sea shanties (work songs; 'The Wellerman' went viral in 2021, and its 'sugar and tea and rum' is the spec!). Read literally: rum + tea + sugar, a warm or room-temp navy punch; communal, singing strength.

Reef and lagoon: clear warm water, turquoise shallows, bright fish. Read as light and translucent aqua: white rum, lime, coconut water, a touch of blue curaçao (keep the rest clear), lychee or melon for fish-bright fruit; sea-salt drop.

The Mai-Kai's Mystery Drink (Fort Lauderdale, 1956–) arrived with a gong and a dancer; Donn Beach coded his recipes (numbered and lettered syrups) so rivals couldn't copy them. Read as a theatrical bowl whose layers are hard to guess: several rums, a coded house mix (Don's Mix, falernum, Pernod drops), served for two or more with ceremony.

Prohibition rum-running (Rum Row off the US coast, Bill McCoy, 'the real McCoy'); Smuggler's Cove borrowed the mood. Read as strong, aged-rum-forward, a bit clandestine: an old-fashioned-shaped rum drink or a dark sour. (Rum Runner is also a 1972 Islamorada resort drink; don't use that name.)

Kava (ʻawa in Hawaiian): a non-alcoholic, earthy, peppery root drink central to ceremony across Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, Vanuatu and Hawaiʻi; numbs the tongue. Vic's 'Kava Bowl' was just a rum punch. Respectfully: don't mimic the ceremony. Read as earthy-peppery and communal: a low-sugar, earthy bowl (agricole or cachaça, a black-pepper/ginger note), or zero-proof if requested. Kava itself is not in the vocabulary.

Rapa Nui's moai: monumental ancestor figures carved from Rano Raraku tuff, now a favorite tiki mug (popularized by Heyerdahl's Aku-Aku). Read as stoic, monumental, earthy: a strong, stirred or short rum drink with an earthy-smoky edge, served in a Moai mug. Respect the ancestors: no head jokes.

Polynesian wayfinding: navigating by stars, swells and birds; Hōkūleʻa (1976) proved the voyages. Read as long, steady and ocean-bright: a long swizzle or punch of cane spirit, lime, coconut water, honey; navigational stars in the name, not deities.

Steady trade winds and salt air: cooling, fresh, gently salty. Read as a long, light, citrusy highball: rum, grapefruit or lime, soda, a pinch of salt. (Sea Breeze is also a vodka-cranberry-grapefruit highball; avoid the name.)

Dragons: fire, hoard, scales, power. Read as fiery and smoky with a jewel-red or gold glow: chili/ginger heat, smoky rum or mezcal, a red fruit; strong. Five-spice links to Chinese dragon lore. (Dragonfly, Golden Dragon and Formidable Dragon are catalogue names; don't reuse.)

Wizards and potions: arcane herbs, bubbling, color change, mystery. Read as herbal-complex with theater: Chartreuse or Bénédictine with rum, honey, lemon; smoke or a sparkling 'bubbling cauldron' top. Butterbeer (Harry Potter) means butterscotch-cream soda: demerara + butter (hot buttered batter) + vanilla + soda/cream foam. A true color-changing potion needs butterfly-pea tea (missing ingredient).

Unicorns and rainbows: pastel, sparkly, sweet-fruity, whimsical. Read as a light, pastel-pink fruit punch with sparkle: guava or strawberry pink, lychee/elderflower, sparkling wine; if 'rainbow', layer colors (grenadine sinks, a pale middle, a blue float) and say not to stir. Never let blue + red mix into gray-purple.

Outer space: the 1950s–60s space age gave tiki the Saturn (1967) and the Jet Pilot/Test Pilot naming. Read as cool, dark-sky elegant: a gin or light-rum sour with passion fruit and falernum (Saturn-style), served up; 'galaxy' colors (blue-violet) only with butterfly-pea (missing) or a careful blue float, never blue + grenadine mud.

Jet- and space-age tiki: Don the Beachcomber's Test Pilot (1941) and Jet Pilot, the Saturn (1967). Read as a precise, strong, spiced Beachcomber sour, crisp and engineered, served in a footed glass. Never name it Test Pilot, Jet Pilot or Saturn.

Moonlight: silver, cool, nocturnal, romantic. Read as pale and luminous: coconut-white or crystal-clear, vanilla and lychee or a gin-and-rum sour served up; nightcap strength. 'Blue moon' does not demand blue curaçao.

Aliens and UFOs: kitsch green, glowing, weird. Read as playful and strange but well made: an herbal-green or melon-green sour (green Chartreuse or melon liqueur with fresh lime and pineapple), maybe a smoky surprise. Green must come from a green ingredient that's actually in it.

Robots and the future: precision, chrome, clean lines. Read as a clean, precise, minimalist drink: clear or pale, exact proportions (a perfectly balanced Daiquiri-shape), maybe a mechanical metal vessel (julep cup). Cyberpunk adds neon (yuzu, a bright bitter).

Ghosts: pale, translucent, chilling, an anise whisper. Read as pale and eerie: a clear or white drink (egg-white mist, coconut milk), anise drops, a cold daiquiri shape or a white colada; not the dark Zombie.

Zombie apocalypse: here the guest is invoking monsters, and tiki has the answer: the Zombie family (Donn Beach, 1934; 'two per customer'). Strong, multi-rum, grapefruit-cinnamon (Don's Mix), Pernod drops, falernum, a 151 float. Name it something new; never 'Zombie'.

Vampires: blood-red, velvet, night, aristocratic. Read as deep blood-red and silky: pomegranate/hibiscus or cherry Heering, a dark rum, a bitter-aristocratic edge (Campari or amaro), served up in a coupe. Not a Bloody Mary.
Werewolves: wild, forest, smoke, primal. Read as smoky, peppery and feral: rye or mezcal with rum, ginger, a bitter herbal snarl; dark amber.

Witches and cauldrons: herbal, dark, bubbling, autumnal. Read as herbal-dark: amaro or Chartreuse with dark rum, apple or blackberry, spice; a bubbling ginger-beer top for the cauldron. (Bewitched Blossom is a catalogue name.)

The Kraken: Norse sea monster turned black-rum legend (there's also a Kraken black spiced rum brand: don't name it). Read as abyssal and ink-dark: black blended rum, molasses, spice, lime, a heavyweight Zombie or grog in a tall glass; a dark float spreading like ink.

Fairies and enchanted woods: floral, green, delicate, a little mischief. Read as light, floral and herbal: elderflower, mint, cucumber, gin or agricole, honey; pale green only from herbs; flower garnish.
taglineWords: found in a ring of mushrooms

concepts.reading: The phoenix: fire and rebirth, gold-red plumage. Read as a fiery, golden-red bird: passion fruit and grenadine sunrise, ginger heat, a flamed garnish; a nod to the Jungle Bird lineage for 'bird'.
The yeti: snowy, shaggy, frosty-white. Read as a frosty white frozen drink: coconut, vanilla, a hint of mint or cinnamon, blended snowy, served in a big mug.

Atlantis: a sunken civilization, ruins, deep blue. Read as cool, deep and mysterious: a blue-to-dark gradient is possible only with layering (blue curaçao base, clear body); otherwise a pale saline gin-and-rum sour with an herbal depth.

The ghost ship (Flying Dutchman legend): fog, rotting sails, a skeleton crew. Read as foggy and spectral-dark: a Fog Cutter-ish orgeat punch with a dark float, anise mist, or a smoky navy grog. Never name it Fog Cutter.
The genie and the lamp: spice-market, smoke, gold, wishes. Read as spice-market gold: honey, orange-flower water, cinnamon, a smoke curl; aged rum or brandy; served in a snifter or tulip.

A trip back in time: 'vintage', 'old school', 'retro'. Read as golden-age authenticity: a 1930s–50s Beachcomber or Vic-style recipe with honest ingredients (honey mix, Don's Mix, falernum, orgeat, two or three rums), period glass or mug. No blue liqueurs or schnapps.

Superheroes: bold, powerful, colorful, bigger-than-life. Read as bold and punchy: a strong, vivid drink with a clear hero flavor (passion fruit or pineapple), high-impact garnish; strength up. Comic/trademark names stay out of the drink name.

Greco-Roman sea gods (Poseidon/Neptune, the trident): fair game for a bit of grandeur. Read as regal-oceanic: a three-rum ('trident') grog or swizzle with lime, honey and a saline edge, cold and deep.

'For my wine-loving mom': bridge from wine. Use fortified and aromatized wines (Lillet, amontillado, sweet vermouth, port) or a sparkling-wine crown, lighter rum or brandy, fresh citrus and fruit; low to moderate proof, elegant glass (coupe, flute, tulip). A tiki cobbler or a sherry-touched punch, not a sugar bomb. Without 'wine', 'mom' alone shouldn't force anything.

A wine drinker: values acidity, dryness, aromatics, food-friendliness. Use wine and fortified wine as modifiers (sherry, Lillet, port, vermouth, sparkling), dry citrus balance, moderate proof; a punch or cobbler.

For grandparents: nostalgic, gentle, recognisable: brandy, sherry, bourbon or a mid-century tropical (a 1950s resort punch, a Brandy-based Scorpion cup). Moderate sweetness and strength, smaller pour, no novelty colors. Respect: age doesn't mean sweet; let other words lead.
taglineWords: the way they poured it in '58

concepts.reading: A tiki newcomer: start with an approachable icon structure (Mai Tai-, Daiquiri- or Painkiller-shaped), recognisable flavors (lime, pineapple, orange, almond, coconut), one or two rums, moderate strength, no overproof bite or absinthe rinse, a fun garnish. Explain the family lineage so they learn. (Malihini = newcomer in Hawaiian.)

A whiskey drinker: give them tiki through their spirit. Precedents: Vic's Honi Honi (bourbon Mai Tai), the Port Light (bourbon, passion fruit, lemon), the Eastern Sour, the Paniolo Old Fashioned. Bourbon or rye as base, a tropical modifier (falernum, allspice, passion fruit, orgeat), spirit-forward balance.
taglineWords: for the whiskey side of the bar

concepts.reading: Someone who hates rum: tiki without rum has deep precedent: gin (Saturn, Vic's gin drinks), bourbon (Honi Honi, Port Light), brandy (Scorpion components), tequila/mezcal (craft-era riffs), aquavit, pisco. Exclude every rum and rum-based liqueur (coconut rum, spiced rum, Swedish punsch); keep tiki modifiers.

A gin drinker: botanicals and dryness. Tiki-gin precedents: the Saturn (1967), Vic's Fog Cutter/Scorpion (gin in support), the Singapore Sling, Suffering Bastard. Gin base, passion fruit/falernum/orgeat, lemon, crisp; or a gin swizzle.
taglineWords: for the gin side of the bar

concepts.reading: An agave lover: tequila or mezcal in tiki skeletons is well established in the craft era (Tiki Margaritas, mezcal Mai Tais, Pirate King Punch's tequila base). Agave base, lime, passion fruit/pineapple, falernum or orgeat, chili optional; salt welcome.

A vodka drinker likes clean, neutral, uncomplicated. Tiki precedent: the Chi Chi (vodka colada) and Harry Yee's Blue Hawaii (vodka + rum). Use vodka as base (or white rum as a gentle step), fresh fruit, crisp citrus, low funk; no overproof.

A beer drinker: long, refreshing, bitter-edged, effervescent. Ginger beer bucks and grog-with-soda are the bridge (beer itself is a missing ingredient: a tiki shandy would need lager). Long, dry-ish, bitter hint, fizzy; not creamy.

For a bartender: they want something they haven't had, made with care: unusual but logical (bitter, agricole, aquavit, Batavia arrack, sherry), restrained sweetness, technique respected, a nod to a deep-cut precedent. Fernet or amaro has industry-handshake status. Not sweet, not gimmicky.
taglineWords: for the other side of the bar

concepts.reading: A tiki aficionado (Beachbum Berry / Smuggler's Cove literate): blended rums by category (Cate's taxonomy), Donn Beach seasoning (Don's Mix, falernum, Pernod drops, Angostura), fresh juice, correct dilution and ice, a period-correct vessel. Deep-cut riff with lineage; never blue liqueurs, sour mix or coconut rum.

To impress: theatre plus quality. A flaming spent-lime shell or Volcano Bowl, a striking vessel (Scorpion bowl, pineapple, skull), a layered float, a dramatic garnish (orchid + mint bouquet + cherry); but the recipe must still be balanced, and makeable at home (no rare ingredients).

phrases: not a fan of strong drinks
concepts.reading: For someone who likes sweet drinks or dislikes the taste of alcohol: lower proof, more juice and creaminess, softer rums (light, Barbados), fruit-forward (pineapple, passion fruit, coconut, banana), still balanced with acid. Be honest in the explanation that strength hides well in juicy drinks.

A zero-proof guest: build a real tiki drink without spirits, not just juice: complex syrups (Don's Mix, falernum syrup, orgeat, passion fruit, cinnamon, honey), fresh citrus, a tea or ginger backbone for 'bite', soda or ginger beer for length, full garnish ceremony. Exclude everything with ABV (including bitters by the dash only if the guest's reason allows; for pregnancy or kids, omit bitters and vanilla extract).
taglineWords: all of the ceremony, none of the proof

concepts.reading: A bitter lover: the Jungle Bird lineage (Campari + dark rum + pineapple), Trinidad Sour (Angostura as base), Kingston Negroni, amaro-tiki. Bitter tiki family, low sugar, rich rum.
A coffee lover: Coffee Grog and Kona traditions; coffee as a real component (cold brew or espresso, coffee liqueur), aged rum, warm spice, low acid. Hot or cold.

A culinary audience: savory-leaning balance, interesting texture, salt as seasoning, food-friendly acidity and moderate sugar. Saline, sherry, herbs (basil, cucumber), fresh ginger; a sour or swizzle that pairs with food.

Lower-sugar request: cut syrups and liqueurs, lean on fresh citrus, soda/coconut water length, aromatics (mint, ginger, bitters) and a smaller pour; avoid cream of coconut and nectar. Be honest: alcohol has calories too.

For a partner or date: don't stereotype by gender ('for my girlfriend' does not mean pink and sweet; 'for my husband' does not mean whiskey). Read as elegant, shareable, conversation-starting: a balanced, aromatic drink in a beautiful glass or a bowl for two, moderate strength.

A group: batchable, crowd-pleasing, bowl or pitcher service, moderate proof (people drink more than one), familiar flavors, plenty of ice and a dramatic communal vessel. Avoid divisive ingredients (absinthe rinse, Islay, heavy bitter).

Sophisticated and safe: polished, not kitschy; a clear, elegant, balanced drink in a coupe or rocks glass; moderate strength, low novelty, quality aged rum or a refined gin sour. Garnish restrained (a twist, an orchid at most).
Budget/college: common, cheap bottles only (cost 1), few ingredients, batchable, fun; never compromise fresh lime. Moderate proof (responsibility).

A Scotch drinker: smoke and malt. Tiki precedents use Scotch sparingly (Islay floats on a Penicillin-like tiki sour, Scotch in Vic-era 'Mai Tai' variants is rare). Blended Scotch base with honey, ginger, lemon; an Islay float; maybe falernum.
A brandy drinker: Trader Vic loved brandy (Scorpion, Fog Cutter). Brandy base or co-base with rum, orgeat, orange, lemon, a sherry float: the orgeat-punch family.

Someone who wants real heat: chili (Ancho Reyes, fresh jalapeño), fresh ginger, black pepper; balanced with fruit (pineapple, mango, passion fruit) and lime so it's not just burn. Tell them the heat level.

Silky: rounded mouthfeel without being thick. Achieved with egg white (shaken dry first), a little coconut milk, orgeat or honey, gum/pineapple syrup, Velvet falernum, and less sharp acid; aged rum over overproof. Not necessarily creamy-opaque.
Velvety: richer than silky: cream of coconut, cream, egg, PX sherry or butter batter, aged and dark rums, warm spice. Dense but still balanced.

Fizzy: carbonation is the texture. Top (never shake) with soda, ginger beer, tonic or sparkling wine; build tall over ice; keep the shaken base slightly over-concentrated to survive the top. A Grog with soda, a Swizzle with a sparkling crown, or a Buck.

Frosty: the glass frosts and the drink runs very cold: swizzled on crushed ice in a metal cup or collins (Queen's Park Swizzle, julep), or flash-blended/frozen. Mint and cooling flavors help; keep sugar a touch higher since cold dulls sweetness.

Frozen/blended: blend with crushed ice to a sorbet texture; increase sugar and flavor intensity (cold and dilution mute both), include fruit or coconut for body. Families: frozen Daiquiri, Colada, resort punch.

Fiery: actual heat. Chili (Ancho Reyes, muddled jalapeño), fresh ginger, black pepper/five-spice, cinnamon; balance with sugar, fruit and lime so heat reads as pleasant. Not to be confused with 'warming' (spice/boozy) or 'hot' (temperature).

Warming: baking spice, aged spirits and maybe heat. Either a hot drink (Hot Buttered Rum, Coffee Grog, hot punch) or a stirred spiced nightcap; allspice, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, demerara, honey; dark rums.
Bracing: high acid and dryness with a clean finish: extra lime/grapefruit, less sugar, a dry rum or agricole, bitters; served very cold, short. Daiquiri/Grog territory.
Refreshing: long, cold, lightly sweet, bright acid, aromatic (mint, cucumber, ginger), lower proof; coconut water or soda; crushed ice. A Swizzle, Buck or long Grog.

Boozy/spirit-forward: more spirit, less juice; stirred or a short sour with an overproof component kept to the dose classics use (¾–1 oz 151). Zombie and stirred families. Warn about strength in the explanation.
Light: low proof, low body, high aromatics: white rum or agricole, bright citrus, soda or coconut water, a floral/herbal touch; no dairy or dark rum.
Dessert-like: creamy or rich, sweeter, low acid, warm notes (vanilla, chocolate, caramel, coffee, banana, coconut). Colada or stirred/flip structures, smaller pour.
Frothy: a foam cap from egg white (dry shake), aquafaba, or a hard-shaken pineapple juice (pineapple foams naturally) or flash-blend; a sour structure, served up or in a pilsner.
Smooth: no harsh edges: aged/column rums rather than overproof or funky pot still, enough sugar and dilution, rounded modifiers (orgeat, honey, vanilla). Moderate proof.
Dry: minimal residual sugar; push acid-to-sugar ratio toward a Daiquiri's 8:1 or drier, use dry modifiers (dry curaçao, amontillado, dry vermouth, bitters), avoid nectars and cream of coconut.
Juicy: fruit-forward, mouth-filling: real juices and nectars (pineapple, passion fruit, mango, guava, orange), longer build, moderate proof; resort punch or Punch family.
Minty-cool: lots of fresh mint (spanked, not shredded), crushed ice, lime; a Swizzle (Queen's Park) or Julep-cup build; optionally a Fernet/Chartreuse accent. Pale green only from mint itself.
Salty/briny: a saline solution (a few drops, not a rim's worth) lifts fruit and dulls bitterness; amontillado and Islay bring brine; li hing mui is salty-sweet-sour. Keep it seasoning, not soup.
taglineWords: with a pinch of sea salt

concepts.reading: Bittersweet: sugar and bitterness held in tension: Campari/Aperol/amaro with pineapple and dark rum (Jungle Bird), or Angostura-forward.

Tingly/numbing: Sichuan peppercorn or buzz-button (spilanthes) flowers make the mouth buzz; neither is in the vocabulary (missing). Approximate with five-spice syrup (contains Sichuan pepper), fresh ginger and effervescence; say it's an approximation.
Full-bodied: dark and Demerara rums, rich syrups (demerara 2:1), PX or cream of coconut, honey/butter; heavier pour; colada or stirred.

A stronger drink (not 'the strongest'): raise spirit share within the family's ABV band, trim juice and lengtheners, add a measured overproof component (¼–½ oz) rather than doubling everything; keep balance by trimming sugar proportionally.

Lower proof, built for several rounds: long builds with soda or coconut water, fortified/aromatized wines (Lillet, sherry) splitting the base, bright citrus and fruit. Target well under 10% ABV after dilution.

Sweeter: raise sugar a notch within the family window (toward ~12–14:1 sugar:acid), prefer flavorful sweeteners (honey, demerara, fruit syrups, cream of coconut) over plain syrup; never drop acid to zero.
Tarter: push toward the Daiquiri's ~8:1 sugar:acid; add lime or grapefruit, cut nectars; keep a little sugar so it doesn't taste thin.

Complex: Donn Beach's method: two or three rums by category, a secret seasoning (Don's Mix, falernum, allspice, Pernod drops, Angostura), two citruses, a fruit and a spice syrup; or a bitter/fortified component. Complexity must be legible: each component has a job.

Make-at-home: only common bottles and store-bought or 1:1/2:1 syrups; three to five ingredients; Daiquiri, Grog, Planter's Punch, Painkiller-shaped; no homemade mixes (Don's Mix, gardenia mix), no specialty liqueurs.
taglineWords: from what's already in the cupboard

concepts.reading: Balanced: aim for the family's median chemistry exactly (ABV, sugar, acid), no extremes, no flavor dominating; it's the default, so mostly a request to avoid gimmicks.

Classic-style: golden-age (1934–1960s) technique and pantry: fresh lime and grapefruit, honey mix, Don's Mix, falernum, orgeat, curaçao, two or three rums by category, crushed ice, flash blend; Don's or Vic's structures. No blue liqueur, schnapps, sour mix or coconut rum.

Modern/craft: revival-era balance (fresh, strong, measured), inversions and unusual bases (Angostura as base, Chartreuse, mezcal, aquavit, sherry), bitter elements, precise garnish; clean presentation over kitsch.

Crowd-pleaser: the famous-drink profile from the catalogue (longer, gentler ~12% ABV, slightly sweeter, five ingredients): pineapple, lime, orange, almond or coconut, two familiar rums; no divisive bitters, smoke or anise.

Hangover: tiki has the canonical cure, Joe Scialom's Suffering Bastard (Shepheard's Hotel, Cairo, 1942): gin, brandy, lime, Angostura, ginger beer. Read as a ginger-beer buck: hydrating, gingery, bitters, lower proof, maybe a coffee or coconut-water element. Don't reuse 'Suffering Bastard'; 'Corpse Reviver' is a classic name too.

Pretty/colorful: color from real ingredients only (passion fruit gold, guava/hibiscus pink, grenadine sinking red, Campari red, mint green, blue curaçao only with clear partners), a clean layer or float, and a flower-and-fruit garnish; a glass that shows the color.
Huge: volume, not necessarily proof. A bowl (Scorpion, Tiki Bowl) or a 20 oz hurricane/pineapple with juice and lengtheners; keep ABV moderate.
Small: 3–4 oz finished, served up (Nick & Nora, coupe) or short on a cube; concentrated flavor; a Daiquiri or stirred structure.
Over-the-top: maximal tiki theatre (a garnish bouquet, flaming shell, float, special vessel), up to Zombie-level complexity, still balanced. Pair complexity with a theatrical vessel.
Minimalist: three or four ingredients, one rum, a single precise garnish, served up or on one cube: Daiquiri, Ti' Punch or a stirred rum drink. The rum should be good enough to carry it.

Rum-forward: high spirit share, characterful rums (Jamaican pot still, Demerara, agricole, aged Barbados), little juice; Daiquiri, Ti' Punch, rum Old Fashioned, Mai Tai (which was built to show off rum).

No/low citrus: build balance from other levers: stirred structures (bitters, fortified wine), creamy coladas (fat balances sugar), tea or coffee lengtheners, pineapple's gentle acid only if allowed. Exclude lime, lemon, grapefruit, yuzu, lime cordial, Don's Mix.
A signature drink for an event: batchable, crowd-pleasing, photogenic, moderate proof, a story in the name (use the couple's or event's imagery, not a classic's name); bowl or pre-batched service.
Fast/no equipment: built in the glass over ice (a highball, buck or punch), or stirred in a mixing glass; no egg white, no blending, no homemade syrup.
